entry.title: Future Cop: L.A.P.D., a duel between genres
entry.content:
One of the most fun things I played on the PlayStation was a side mode in a game about police robots. Future Cop: L.A.P.D. came out in 1998, set in a Los Angeles of 2098, and next to its campaign it had a mode called Precinct Assault. Two players, one arena, one base each. You pilot the X1-Alpha, a machine that switches between a fast hover car and a slow, heavily armed walking mech. You drive out to capture turrets and outposts, you spend what they earn on hovertanks that roll toward the other base on their own, and you buy helicopters to shoot down the tanks coming at yours. The first tank to break into a base ends the match.

What made it work was that you were two things at once. You were the soldier, in the middle of the fighting, escorting your tanks through the turrets and hunting the other player. And you were the general, deciding whether the next credits went into attack or defence. Every minute you spent driving back to defend was a minute your own push went without you.

It was not the first game to try this. Herzog Zwei did something close on the Mega Drive in 1989, with a transforming mech of its own, and the Wikipedia article on Future Cop notes that the difference is that you can help your army reach the other base yourself. Precinct Assault is sometimes counted as an early form of the MOBA, and the genre that followed kept the lanes and the units that walk them. But it dropped the economy and the general, and it went from one against one to five against five. I have not found a game since that does exactly what Precinct Assault did.

The version I would like to build is a one-against-one DotA in a setting closer to Terminator: a ruined city, machines on both sides, one transforming unit per player that is both your hero and your commander. Capture a factory and it produces infantry. Capture a ridge and it holds a turret. Everything you own is something the other player can take, and the only way to protect it is to be somewhere, which means not being somewhere else.

References

  • Future Cop: L.A.P.D., Wikipedia.
  • Herzog Zwei, Wikipedia.

entry.title: Gangsters: Organized Crime, orders for the week
entry.content:
The other game I keep coming back to from 1998 is Gangsters: Organized Crime, by Hothouse Creations for Eidos. It is set in New Temperance, a fictional suburb of Chicago during Prohibition, and you start as a small-time crime boss with a handful of hoods and a lot of ambition.

What made it unlike anything else was the rhythm. Each turn you sat down and planned: which lieutenant takes which crew, which shops get visited for protection money, which business opens next. Then you let go, and the working week played out in real time on the city map while you watched your orders meet everyone else’s. Some of it went as planned. Much of it did not, and the next planning session started from whatever the week had left you.

Underneath was a whole small society. Hoods were people with skills, fists and knives and intelligence, recruited from gyms, pool halls and the unemployment office. Money came from protection rackets and from businesses, some legal and some not, and you needed an accountant to launder it and a lawyer to get your people out when they were arrested. Run things carelessly and the police and the FBI started paying attention. And there were three ways to win: take out every rival gang, get yourself elected mayor, or go straight and build a legitimate empire without the law on your back.

That last one is the part I think about most. The same machinery, the hoods, the money, the city, served three different stories, and only one of them was about violence. Most strategy games give you a world to conquer. Gangsters gave you a world to run, with the option of becoming respectable in it.

I have not played anything like it since, and like Precinct Assault, it sits in my head as a design worth picking up again: plan in turns, live with the consequences in real time, and let the player decide what winning means.

References

  • Gangsters: Organized Crime, Wikipedia.
